chunks: Reading UART data without a clock. The question: Since there's no clock, how is data read?
A UART receiver has no clock wire, but it knows how long one bit should last because both sides agreed on the speed.
The line rests high, so a falling edge (a drop from high to low) can only mean "a byte starts now". From that edge the receiver counts time with its own clock.
It reads the line once per bit time, near the middle of each bit.
Picture stepping stones across a stream. You spot the edge of the first stone. You step half a stone in, so you stand in the middle of it.
Then you take strides exactly one stone long, and each lands in the middle of the next stone. The middle is the safest spot, because it is far from both edges.
If your stride is slightly off, the error adds up over ten stones. But once you cross, you restart at the next bank.
One column is half a bit.
The falling edge at the start of the start bit is detected; each rising edge of the "sample" row lands in the middle of a bit cell, so the receiver reads start = 0, D0 = 1, D1.
D5 = 0, D6 = 1, D7 = 0 (that is 0x41, 'A', LSB first) and a high stop bit. The samples are half a bit from every transition.
Start edge: the falling edge that begins a byte. It is the receiver's only timing reference. Bit time: the length of one bit, which is 1 divided by the baud rate.
Mid-bit sampling: reading the line at the middle of each bit, where the signal is steadiest.
Framing error: the stop bit was read low, which usually means the two speeds do not match.
Take 115200 baud, so one bit lasts about 8. 68 microseconds. The receiver sees the line fall at time zero. It waits half a bit, about 4.
34 microseconds, and checks the line is still low. If so, it is a real start bit. Then it reads the line every 8. 68 microseconds: at about 13. 0 microseconds, 21.
7 microseconds, and so on for the eight data bits. The stop bit is read at 9. 5 bit times, about 82. 5 microseconds, and should be high. That is the whole idea.
"The line idles high, so the receiver waits for the falling start edge. From that edge it counts its own bit times using the agreed baud rate.
It waits half a bit to land in the middle of the start bit and confirms it's still low, then samples once per bit time, so every sample lands in the middle of a bit, where the signal is steadiest.
After the data it checks the stop bit is high. Because it re-syncs on every start edge, clock error only builds up over one frame, so up to a few percent mismatch is tolerable."
